publication_scope.blurb: Louis Le Blanc de Beaulieu - Sedan Theological Theses, newly rendered from the 1675 London Latin. Covers De Theologia through Angelorum & Hominum Sanctorum Cultu Romana I-LXXVII and Pars Secunda (Reformata) I-CI, De Primi Hominis Immortalitate I-XXXV, De Justitia Primi Hominis I-LIX, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio in genere I-XLVIII, De Libero Hominis Arbitrio absolute & in se spectato (Scholae Romanae doctrina I-XLIX; Pars Tertia I-XLIII), the theses on reconciling divine concurrence with human freedom I-LIX, on human freedom and divine foreknowledge I-XLIV, and on human freedom and the divine decrees, Part One (middle knowledge) I-LXV, Part Two (the Roman doctors) I-XXXVI and Part Three (the Reformed) I-LI, and on how fallen man's free choice stands toward saving good (I-LX), and on the necessity of grace for moral good in fallen man (Pars Prior I-LIII; Pars Posterior, the Protestant doctrine, I-LIX), and on the various distinctions and senses of grace in the Roman School (I-LXX) and in the Reformed Schools (I-XLIX), and on the Roman School's division of grace into sufficient and efficacious (I-CVII). Not the collected folio.
publication_scope.era_note: Le Blanc wrote in the mid-seventeenth century as Reformed professor at the Academy of Sedan. This is not a patristic work. It is a public-domain Latin Reformed retrieval on the same Fathers-site pipeline. The 1675 Pitt folio is Public Domain Mark 1.0. Do not treat the site as ante-Nicene only.

source_text: XC. Porro quum Doctor iste dicit, si duobus hominibus aequalia auxilia ex parte Dei dentur, fieri posse ut unus pro sua libertate convertatur, & alter non: monet id se intelligere de auxiliis gratiae praevenientis, qua praeveniens est. Nam si agatur de gratiae ejusdem auxiliis, quatenus est cooperans, id est, quatenus per eam Deus influit in actum quem homo libere elicit, non amplius verum est, aequali auxilio dato, unum converti, alterum non converti. Siquidem impossibile est aliquem non converti, & tamen Deum in eo efficere, cum libero ejus arbitrio, conversionis actum. Sed quoniam gratia praeveniens & cooperans reapse sunt unum & idem, & gratiae cooperatio a liberi nostri arbitrii cooperatione pendet, non secus ac concursus & influxus cujusvis habitus, ab operatione potentiae cui inest: simpliciter & absolute loquendo dicendum putat, unum cum aequalibus, aut etiam cum minoribus auxiliis pro sua libertate converti, ac salvari, quando alius neque convertitur neque salvatur. Licet si in summo rigore loquamur, dici non debeat cum aequalibus gratiae auxiliis unum converti, alterum non converti: quoniam in eo qui convertitur est influxus quidam gratiae, qui in alio non est; ille nimirum qui pendet a liberi nostri arbitrii consensu.
english: Thesis XC. When Molina says that if God gives two people equal aids, one may be converted by his own freedom and the other not, he warns that he means the aids of prevenient grace, taken as prevenient. If we speak of that same grace as cooperating, that is, as the grace through which God flows into the act a person freely elicits, it is no longer true that with equal aid one is converted and the other is not. It is impossible for someone not to be converted while God is nevertheless producing in him, together with his free choice, the act of conversion.

Yet prevenient and cooperating grace are in reality one and the same, and the cooperation of grace depends on the cooperation of our free choice, just as the concurrence and influence of any habit depends on the working of the power it resides in. So, speaking simply and absolutely, he thinks one must say that a person is converted and saved by his freedom with equal or even smaller aids, while another is neither converted nor saved. Speaking with the utmost strictness, though, one should not say that with equal aids of grace one is converted and the other not, since in the one converted there is an influence of grace not present in the other: the influence that depends on the consent of our free choice.

source_text: XCI. Similiter juxta hunc Doctorem affirmandum non est, existentibus in duobus adultis aequalibus auxiliis gratiae praevenientis, illum qui convertitur, pro sola sua libertate converti. Quoniam licet conversio illa a libertate pendeat, fiatque ab arbitrio pro sua libertate; non tamen fit pro sola sua libertate, sed cooperante simul auxilio gratiae praevenientis per influxum a quo sortitur rationem gratiae cooperantis: quamvis cum hic praesto sit, gratiamque praevenientem dependenter a cooperatione arbitrii comitetur, solum exigatur cooperatio libera arbitrii nostri. Disputatione quadragesima ad articulum 13. quaestionis 14. paragr. ad secundam.
english: Thesis XCI. In the same way, according to this Doctor, one must not say that when two adults have equal aids of prevenient grace, the one who is converted is converted by his freedom alone. That conversion does depend on freedom and is brought about by choice in its freedom. But it is not brought about by that freedom alone: the aid of prevenient grace cooperates with it at the same time, through the influence by which it takes on the character of cooperating grace.

Even so, when that influence is present and accompanies prevenient grace in dependence on the cooperation of choice, nothing more is required than the free cooperation of our choice. This is in disputation 40 on article 13 of question 14, in the paragraph 'Ad secundam'.

source_text: XCII. Inde vero sequitur, juxta illius hypotheses, positis quibusvis auxiliis gratiae praevenientis, qua praeveniens est, hominem posse non converti, tam in sensu composito, quam in sensu diviso. At posito ejusdem gratiae auxilio, quatenus est cooperans, hominem posse quidem non converti in sensu diviso; Verum id falsum esse in sensu composito; quia fieri non potest, ut adsit influxus gratiae cooperantis, quatenus est cooperans conversionem, quin peccator per suum arbitrium convertatur; quod tamen arbitrii libertati nihil officit: quia influxus iste gratiae cooperantis, ab arbitrii humani consensu, ut saepe jam dictum est, pendet. Ut videre est in eadem disputatione paragr. hinc patet.
english: Thesis XCII. It follows from his assumptions that, whatever aids of prevenient grace are given, taken as prevenient, a person is able not to be converted, in the composite sense as well as in the divided sense. Given the aid of the same grace as cooperating, however, a person can indeed fail to be converted in the divided sense, but not in the composite sense.

For the influence of cooperating grace cannot be present, as cooperating in conversion, without the sinner being converted through his own choice. This takes nothing away from the freedom of choice, because, as has been said many times already, that influence of cooperating grace depends on the consent of human choice. This can be seen in the same disputation, in the paragraph beginning 'Hinc patet'.

source_text: XCIII. Quae sit autem natura divinae illius gratiae, quae diverso respectu praeveniens & cooperans est, & quam liberum hominis arbitrium efficacem vel inefficacem reddit, prolixe explicat Molina disputatione 45. ad articulum 13. quaestionis 14. Et primo quidem in genere gratiam illam constituit in mentis quadam illuminatione, & in motibus quibusdam voluntatis.
english: Thesis XCIII. Molina explains at length, in disputation 45 on article 13 of question 14, the nature of this divine grace, which is prevenient in one respect and cooperating in another, and which man's free choice makes efficacious or inefficacious. To begin with, he places that grace in general in an illumination of the mind and in certain motions of the will.

source_text: XCIV. Ista vero mentis illuminatio ipsi nihil est aliud, quam notitiae quaedam ab externo concionatore, aut aliunde acceptae, & a Deo peculiari, & supernaturali influxu adjutae, ut aliquo modo jam ad salutem accommodatae sint. Observat enim Deum illis quos ordinaria ratione illuminat, non immittere novas species & ideas, quibus fiant cognitiones illae, quarum interventu mens eorum illustratur; sed cognitiones illas fieri per species humano modo acquisitas, & a concionatoribus, aut alia aliqua ratione excitatas, quibus Deus se inserit per suum influxum, ut cognitiones istae ad salutem plus minus accommodatae fiant, pro ratione majoris, vel minoris influxus. Quare, ex ejus sententia, Deum illuminare non aliud est, quam illo modo influxu suo cooperari ad tales cognitiones quibus voluntas excitatur.
english: Thesis XCIV. For him this illumination of the mind is simply a set of notions received from an external preacher or from some other source, and helped by a special, supernatural influence of God so that they are in some way already fitted for salvation. He observes that when God enlightens people in the ordinary way he does not send into them new species and ideas from which that knowledge arises, the knowledge through whose intervention their minds are enlightened.

That knowledge arises through species acquired in the human way and stirred up by preachers or by some other means. God inserts himself into them by his influence, so that this knowledge becomes more or less fitted for salvation, in proportion as his influence is greater or smaller. On Molina's view, then, for God to enlighten is nothing else than to cooperate in this way, by his influence, in the kinds of knowledge that rouse the will.

source_text: XCV. Motus vero voluntatis, in quibus gratia praeveniens consistit, ex illius mente, sunt certi quidam affectus, quibus praevia cognitione, voluntas erigitur, & invitatur, tum ad eliciendam spem, tum ad diligendum Deum, aut dolendum de peccatis, antequam actum spei, aut amoris, vel doloris ex dilectione ejus eliciat. Ad hujusmodi vero motus & affectus non cooperatur voluntas, qua liberum arbitrium est, sed solum qua voluntas, & natura quaedam est. Quippe velit nolit, praesente cognitione, naturaliter in ea insurgunt. Rationem autem gratiae non habent, nisi Deus simul in eosdem specialiter influat, ut evadant supernaturales, & certo quoque modo ad salutem accommodentur.
english: Thesis XCV. On his view the motions of the will that make up prevenient grace are certain affections. Once knowledge has gone before, they raise and invite the will to elicit hope, to love God or to grieve for sins, before it elicits the act of hope, or of love, or of grief arising from love of him.

The will does not cooperate in these motions and affections as free choice, but only as will, that is, as a kind of nature. Whether it wants them or not, they rise up in it naturally once the knowledge is present. They have the character of grace only if God at the same time flows specially into them, so that they become supernatural and are also fitted in a certain way for salvation.

source_text: XCVI. Quod ut plenius intelligi possit, observat ex contemplatione rei valde amabilis, & quam multum refert adipisci, naturaliter consurgere in voluntate motum quendam, quo voluntas ad illam afficitur: qui motus non est volitio, sed affectio voluntatis ad illam rem, a cujus bonitate quasi tangitur & allicitur ad volendum eam. Atque hic motus, juxta ipsum, volitionem antecedere solet, non tantum in hominibus, sed etiam in angelis; idque tam in statu naturae integrae, quam in statu naturae corruptae. Quoniam prius tempore, vel natura fuit Luciferum ad id affici voluntate, quod per superbiam obtinere voluit, quam illud libere vellet. Sicut prius etiam fuit, Evam affici ad pomum vetitum, quam illud comedere vellet contra legem Dei.
english: Thesis XCVI. To make this clearer, he observes that when we contemplate something very lovable and well worth obtaining, a motion rises naturally in the will by which it is drawn toward that thing. This motion is not a volition. It is an affection of the will toward the thing, whose goodness, so to speak, touches it and entices it to will it.

According to Molina this motion normally comes before volition, in angels as well as in men, and in the state of intact nature as well as in that of fallen nature. Lucifer's will was drawn toward what he sought to gain through pride before, in time or in nature, he freely willed it. In the same way Eve was drawn toward the forbidden fruit before she willed to eat it against God's law.

source_text: XCVII. Porro post ejusmodi motum in voluntate ex rei contemplatione exortum, in voluntatis potestate situm est, rem simpliciter velle vel non velle. Sed motus iste, quo ad rem afficitur, non libere, ut jam dictum, sed mere naturaliter in voluntate oritur, posita rei contemplatione. Voluntas tamen indirecte potest hujusmodi motum in se impedire, arcendo nempe cogitationem, & divertendo ad alia, ac procurando ut mens voluntati alia proponat, quae eam ad omnino contraria allicere solent.
english: Thesis XCVII. Once such a motion has arisen in the will from contemplating the thing, it is in the will's power simply to will the thing or not to will it. The motion by which the will is drawn toward the thing, however, does not arise freely, as was said; it arises in the will purely by nature once the thing is contemplated.

Still, the will can hinder that motion in itself indirectly: by keeping the thought away, by turning to other matters, and by seeing to it that the mind sets before the will other things that usually draw it toward the very opposite.

source_text: XCVIII. Quod si existente affectu ad aliquam rem, quam mens ut amabilem concipit, & voluntati offert, menti occurrat via & aditus, quo obtineri posse credatur, naturaliter etiam consurgit in voluntate motus quidam quasi erectionis illius ad sperandum, qui tempore, vel natura, antecedit actum liberum spei. Adeoque motus ille a notitia bonitatis objecti, & notitia viae qua obtineri posse creditur, cooperante voluntate, non ut libera, sed natura quaedam est, efficitur; exurgitque naturaliter in voluntate, eo major, quo notitia bonitatis objecti, & viae qua obtineri possit, major & verisimilior est, sicuti se res habet in affectu illo voluntatis ad objectum cognitum simpliciter ut bonum.
english: Thesis XCVIII. Suppose there is an affection toward something that the mind conceives as lovable and presents to the will, and the mind then sees a way and an approach by which it believes the thing can be obtained. A motion then also rises naturally in the will, a kind of uplift toward hoping, which comes before the free act of hope in time or in nature.

That motion is produced by the knowledge of the object's goodness and the knowledge of the way it is believed it can be obtained, with the will cooperating not as free but as a kind of nature. It rises naturally in the will, and it is the stronger, the greater and more probable is the knowledge of the object's goodness and of the way to obtain it. The same holds for the will's affection toward an object known simply as good.

source_text: XCIX. Jam autem Doctor ille non aliud gratiae tribuit quam ut perficiat naturam, eamque adjuvet in suis motibus, ut unusquisque ex supernaturali auxilio & gratia talis sit, qualis ad salutem oportet. Ac proinde ad dignoscendos & explicandos motus gratiae, vult attendi ad progressum & ordinem, quem natura ipsa, potentiaeve cognoscentes & appetentes servarent, si illos eosdem actus, qui gratiae tribuuntur, suis solis viribus quoad substantiam actus producerent, quod fieri posse ille existimat. Ut ea ratione intelligatur quo pacto Deus per auxilia ac dona gratiae, se inserat & cooperetur cum natura, eamque adjuvet, ut supra suas vires eos actus producat quales ad salutem necessarii sunt.
english: Thesis XCIX. Molina gives grace no other role than to perfect nature and help it in its own motions, so that each person becomes, through supernatural aid and grace, what salvation requires. To identify and explain the motions of grace, therefore, he wants us to look at the course and order that nature itself, or the knowing and desiring powers, would follow if they produced, by their own strength alone, the substance of the same acts that are attributed to grace. He thinks this can happen.

In this way we are to understand how God, through the aids and gifts of grace, inserts himself into nature, cooperates with it and helps it, so that it produces beyond its own strength such acts as are necessary for salvation.

source_text: C. Itaque motus illos in quibus constituit gratiam praevenientem, censet esse operationes vitales, a facultatibus nostris active procedentes, sed quae tamen libere ab eis non eliciuntur, nec dici debent actus liberi arbitrii, proprie loquendo, quanquam multum a libero arbitrio pendeant. Idque quoniam liberum arbitrium variis modis potest actus illos juvare, vel impedire, eosque desiderare & petere a Deo, & quodammodo seipsum aptare & disponere, ut juxta communem cursum & ordinem divinae providentiae, facilius sibi a Deo donentur.
english: Thesis C. So he holds that the motions in which he places prevenient grace are vital operations proceeding actively from our faculties. Yet they are not elicited freely by those faculties, and strictly speaking they should not be called acts of free choice, though they depend a great deal on free choice.

The reason is that free choice can help or hinder those acts in various ways, can desire them and ask God for them, and can in some way fit and dispose itself so that, by the common course and order of divine providence, they may be given to it by God more readily.

source_text: CI. Exempli gratia, notitiae illae rerum credendarum, quibus accedente quodam influxu supernaturali, mens nostra salutariter illustrari incipit, libere comparari possunt, aurem praebendo concionatoribus, & libros pios evolvendo, aliave simili quapiam ratione: ut & ab eis potest aliquis sese libere avertere, & ita divinae illuminationi obstaculum ponere: Licet notitiae illae rationem gratiae praevenientis obtineant, solum ab influxu Dei supernaturali, non vero a libero hominis arbitrio. Et eodem modo pii illi affectus, qui posita Dei illuminatione, naturaliter & necessario in voluntate resultant, & qui rationem habent gratiae praevenientis, ex parte voluntatis, si peculiaris quidam Dei influxus ad eos accedat, possunt a libero hominis arbitrio impediri, dum homo libere cessat a pia cogitatione, aut adducit & quaerit rationes allicientes voluntatem in partem oppositam; & contra juvari, si quis mentem ultro retineat in pia illa cogitatione.
english: Thesis CI. For example, the notions of things to be believed, through which, with a supernatural influence added, our mind begins to be enlightened for salvation, can be acquired freely: by listening to preachers, by reading devout books, or in some similar way. Equally, a person can freely turn away from them and so put an obstacle in the way of God's illumination. Even so, those notions get the character of prevenient grace only from God's supernatural influence, not from man's free choice.

The same is true of the devout affections that result naturally and necessarily in the will once God's illumination is given, and that have the character of prevenient grace on the will's side if some special influence of God is added to them. Man's free choice can hinder them, when he freely stops thinking devout thoughts or brings up and looks for reasons that draw the will the other way. It can also help them, when someone of his own accord keeps his mind fixed on that devout thought.

source_text: CII. Sed ut clarius pateat quae sit Molinae sententia, non alienum erit verbis ipsius exponere ordinem & rationem motuum gratiae praevenientis, qua vocamur ad fidem, spem, dilectionem, & contritionem, quibus hominis conversio constat. Sic ergo jam dicta disputatione ea de re philosophatur. Dum homo, inquit, nondum ad fidem supernaturaliter interius vocatus, cogitat & expendit res credendas, per notitias concionatoris ministerio, aut aliunde comparatas, influit Deus in easdem notitias influxu quodam particulari ac supernaturali, quo cognitionem illam adjuvat, tum ut res melius & dilucidius expendatur, & penetretur, tum etiam ut notitia illa jam limites notitiae supernaturalis, & ad finem supernaturalem in suo ordine & gradu accommodatae attingat. Ex cognitione vero & penetratione earum rerum quae ad fidem spectant, nempe quum expenditur quam digne sint quibus assensus adhibeatur, quantumque id expediat, oritur naturaliter in voluntate motus affectionis ad res ita cognitas, quo allicitur, & quasi invitatur, ad imperandum intellectui assensum, quo eis assentiatur. Cum hoc ergo motu quasi se inserit etiam Deus; influens in illum per auxilium particulare, illumque eo auxilio quasi acuit, ut magis urgeat & alliciat, efficitque illum supernaturalem, ut in suo ordine & gradu sit etiam ad salutem accommodatus.
english: Thesis CII. To show Molina's view more clearly, it will be to the point to set out in his own words the order and pattern of the motions of prevenient grace by which we are called to faith, hope, love and contrition, in which a person's conversion consists. In the disputation already cited he reasons about this as follows.

'While a person not yet inwardly called to faith in a supernatural way thinks over and weighs the things to be believed, through notions acquired by a preacher's ministry or from some other source,' he says, 'God flows into those notions by a particular, supernatural influence. By it he helps that knowledge, so that the matter is weighed better and more clearly and is penetrated, and also so that the knowledge now reaches the level of supernatural knowledge, fitted in its order and degree to a supernatural end.

When the mind weighs and enters into the things that belong to faith, that is, how worthy they are of assent and how much it matters to assent, a motion of affection toward the things so known arises naturally in the will. By it the will is drawn and, so to speak, invited to command the intellect to assent to them. God too, as it were, inserts himself into this motion. He flows into it through a particular aid and with that aid as it were sharpens it, so that it presses and draws more strongly, and he makes it supernatural, so that in its order and degree it is fitted for salvation as well.'

source_text: CIII. Porro liberum arbitrium his duobus motibus gratiae praevenientis adjutum & excitatum, liberam adhuc habet potestatem imperandi, aut non imperandi assensum fidei. Quod si voluntas fidem amplecti velit, actumque credendi imperet intellectui, influente simul motu gratiae praevenientis, quam habet, elicit in seipsa actum supernaturalem, quo fidem amplecti vult, quoque assensum imperat intellectui: simulque intellectus motus imperio illo supernaturali voluntatis, illustrationeque divina adjutus, elicit actum supernaturalem assentiendi revelatis, hisque duobus actibus supernaturalibus intellectus & voluntatis homo rite dispositus suscipit habitum fidei supernaturalem, a Deo solo infusum, quo deinceps similes actus supernaturales valeat producere.
english: Thesis CIII. 'Even when these two motions of prevenient grace have helped and roused it, free choice remains free to command the assent of faith or to withhold that command. Suppose the will decides to embrace the faith and orders the intellect to believe. Then, as the motion of prevenient grace it possesses flows in alongside, the will produces within itself a supernatural act: in that act it wills to embrace the faith, and by that act it orders the intellect to assent.

In the same moment the intellect, set in motion by the will's supernatural command and aided by God's light, produces a supernatural act of assent to what God has revealed. A person rightly prepared by these two supernatural acts, one of intellect and one of will, then receives from God alone the infused, supernatural habit of faith, which enables him afterwards to produce further acts of the same supernatural kind.'

source_text: CIV. Quod spectat gratiae motum, quo ad spei actum excitamur, sic mentem suam de illo explicat. Dum intellectus, inquit, illustratus jam lumine fidei supernaturalis, sempiternam beatitudinem homini a Deo praeparatam cogitat, bonitatem ac excellentiam illius, tum multa alia & praeclara Dei opera, ac beneficia in hominem collata, de quorum numero sunt Christi incarnatio ac passio, consideratque reliqua media quae sibi ad vitam aeternam consequendam abundantissime suppeditata sunt, naturaliter oritur in voluntate non solum affectus ad beatitudinem, quo allicitur & invitatur ut eam amore concupiscentiae velit, sed etiam motus erectionis, quo attrahitur & allicitur ad eam ipsam a Deo sperandam. Quamvis autem hic motus a libero arbitrio pendeat, si a cogitatione ex qua motus oritur cesset; nihilominus sublatis impedimentis, mere naturaliter insurgit, eique quasi se ingerit Deus specialiter influendo, eumque acuit & efficit supernaturalem, ut in suo ordine & gradu sit qualis ad salutem necessarius est; per eumque supernaturaliter erigit, & quasi invitat voluntatem, ut eliciat actum supernaturalem sperandi sempiternam beatitudinem, & media ad illam comparandam necessaria. Per ejusmodi ergo gratiam liberum nostrum arbitrium, a Deo praeventum & excitatum elicit, si vult, primum actum spei supernaturalis liberum, quo rite dispositum consequitur a Deo habitum spei supernaturalis, per quem in posterum elicere possit alios similes actus supernaturales quotiescunque voluerit.
english: Thesis CIV. On the motion of grace that rouses us to the act of hope, he explains his view as follows. 'When the intellect, already enlightened by the light of supernatural faith, thinks about the eternal happiness God has prepared for man, about its goodness and excellence, about God's many other glorious works and the benefits he has conferred on man, among them Christ's incarnation and passion, and considers the other means most abundantly supplied to it for gaining eternal life, there arises naturally in the will not only an affection toward happiness, by which the will is drawn and invited to want it with love of desire, but also a motion of uplift, by which it is attracted and drawn to hope for that happiness from God.

This motion does depend on free choice, if choice turns away from the thought from which the motion arises. Nevertheless, once obstacles are removed, it rises purely by nature, and God, as it were, thrusts himself into it with a special influence. He sharpens it and makes it supernatural, so that in its order and degree it is what salvation requires, and through it he raises the will supernaturally and, so to speak, invites it to elicit the supernatural act of hoping for eternal happiness and for the means needed to gain it.

Through such grace, then, our free choice, anticipated and roused by God, elicits, if it wishes, the first free act of supernatural hope. Duly disposed by that act, it receives from God the habit of supernatural hope, through which it can afterwards elicit other similar supernatural acts whenever it chooses.'

source_text: CV. Quibus consentanea quoque circa gratiam ad actum Dilectionis Dei, & contritionis de peccatis necessariam edisserit. Deinde, inquit, quum intellectus lumine fidei illustratus, praeexistenteque actu spei supernaturalis in voluntate, Dei bonitatem tum secundum se, tum erga nos considerat, & tam multa ac magna beneficia quibus tam suaviter nos praevenit, naturaliter excitatur in voluntate motio amoris amicitiae erga Deum quo ea potentia allicitur, & ad Deum diligendum invitatur. Huic etiam motui se inserit Deus, illumque suo supernaturali influxu, non solum acuit & incendit, sed etiam efficit supernaturalem, qualis videlicet, in suo ordine & gradu est ad salutem necessarius.
english: Thesis CV. In keeping with this he also discusses the grace needed for the act of love of God and of contrition for sins. 'Next,' he says, 'when the intellect, enlightened by the light of faith, with an act of supernatural hope already present in the will, considers God's goodness both in itself and toward us, and the many great benefits with which he has gone before us so gently, a motion of the love of friendship toward God is stirred up naturally in the will.

By that motion the power is drawn and invited to love God. God inserts himself into this motion too, and by his supernatural influence he not only sharpens and kindles it but also makes it supernatural, of the kind, that is, which in its order and degree is necessary for salvation.'

source_text: CVI. Quod si simul accedat cognitio magnitudinis, multitudinis, atque ingratitudinis peccatorum, quibus Deum offendimus, liberum arbitrium gratia eadem praeventum, ut elicere potest actum dilectionis Dei supernaturalis, ita poterit elicere actum veri doloris de peccatis, propter Deum ex affectu amoris supernaturalis dilectum, qui est vera contritio, & ultima dispositio ad gratiam gratum facientem, quae in eodem instanti, posterius tamen natura, contritionem ipsam consequitur.
english: Thesis CVI. 'If, at the same time, knowledge is added of how great, how many and how ungrateful are the sins by which we offend God, then free choice, anticipated by the same grace, just as it can elicit the act of supernatural love of God, so will be able to elicit the act of true sorrow for sins, felt on account of God, who is loved with an affection of supernatural love.
That sorrow is true contrition and the final disposition for sanctifying grace, which follows contrition in the same instant, though later in the order of nature.'

source_text: CVII. Caeterum autor ille distinguit inter auxilium gratiae praevenientis, & inter gratiam ipsam praevenientem. Et quidem per gratiam praevenientem intelligit illas cognitiones mentis, & affectiones voluntatis, quas Deus influxu quodam particulari acuit & adjuvat, ut fiant supernaturales; & in gradu & ordine suo, quales ad salutem oportet. Per auxilium vero gratiae praevenientis intelligit influxum illum supernaturalem, quo Deus cognitiones istas, humana ut plurimum ratione acquisitas, & affectiones, posita ejusmodi cognitione mere naturaliter in voluntate insurgentes, quo modo dictum est, acuit, adjuvat & incendit, ut evadant supernaturales, & quales ad aeternam hominis salutem conducit.
english: Thesis CVII. Molina also distinguishes the aid of prevenient grace from prevenient grace itself. By prevenient grace he means the knowledge in the mind and the affections in the will that God sharpens and helps by a particular influence so that they become supernatural and, in their degree and order, what salvation requires.

By the aid of prevenient grace he means the supernatural influence by which God sharpens, helps and kindles that knowledge, mostly acquired by human means, and those affections, which, as described, rise purely by nature in the will once such knowledge is present. Through it they become supernatural and of the kind that serves man's eternal salvation.
